concept.name: Call option
concept.definition: A call option is a contract that gives its buyer (holder) the right, but not the obligation, to purchase a specified quantity of an underlying asset or to enter a long futures position at a specified strike price on or before a specified expiration date. The option writer (seller) has the corresponding obligation to sell the underlying if the holder exercises.
concept.intuition: Buying a call is like paying a small fee to lock in a purchase price: if the asset rises above that price you can buy it cheap, and if it doesn't you simply walk away, losing only the fee.
concept.mechanics: The buyer pays a premium to the writer. At expiration a call is worth its intrinsic value max(S - K, 0); before expiration it also carries time value reflecting volatility, time remaining, rates, and dividends. American-style calls may be exercised any time before expiry; European-style only at expiry.
concept.formula: Payoff at expiration (long call) = max(S_T - K, 0); profit = max(S_T - K, 0) - premium, where S_T is the underlying price at expiration and K is the strike price.
concept.failure_modes: Buyers routinely overpay for time value: even a correct directional view loses money if the move is smaller or later than the premium implies (volatility crush, time decay). Sellers face theoretically unlimited loss on uncovered calls.
concept.misconceptions: A call is not 'leveraged stock ownership': the holder has no voting rights or dividends and the contract can expire worthless. Nor is exercise the usual exit; most listed calls are closed by offsetting sale.
concept.example: Buy one XYZ $100 call for a $3 premium (contract = 100 shares, cost $300). If XYZ finishes at $110 at expiration, the call is worth $10 and profit is ($10 - $3) x 100 = $700; if XYZ finishes at or below $100, the loss is the full $300 premium.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
